newsitem.title: UK: Mark bulls resist wide EMU talk before French vote.
newsitem.headline: Mark bulls resist wide EMU talk before French vote.

text.p: Mark bulls are putting the best spin they can on both the row that has erupted between the Bundesbank and the German government and the prospect France will push for a broad economic and monetary union after Sunday's election.

Traders are focusing on the chances a victory for France's opposition Socialist party will lead to a delay in EMU, with the beleaguered German government already fighting a rearguard action against its own central bank over Bonn's plans to revalue its assets.

Germany's internal dispute has made it less able to resist French demands that Italy and Spain join EMU from the outset. The mark and Swiss franc are benefiting as traders bet Germany would rather postpone EMU than replace the mark with a potentially softer euro.
Mark gains will be short-lived, though, if Germany and France close ranks in their determination to launch EMU on time in 1999, bringing convergence plays back into vogue.
"The political will is so great that EMU will go ahead anyway," said Ian Winship, a fund manager at Scottish Amicable Investment Managers.
"It will be easier for the French and the Italians to bend the rules slightly given the problems the Germans are having,'' he said. "People really should be looking for a wider EMU."

The mark stood at 3.3795/00 French francs at 1226 GMT versus 3.3804/09 late Thursday in Europe. It rose to a one-month high of 995.25 Italian lire from 991.90/2.20 Thursday, before settling at 994.30.
The mark is expected to get a fillip against the French franc in the immediate aftermath of the election if the Socialists win power.
Its gains will be limited, though, both by central bank intervention and because it will leave Germany more isolated in its desire to found EMU with a select group of countries.
Lionel Jospin, the leader of the Socialists, has called for Italy and Spain to be founding members of EMU and for more emphasis to be placed on growth.

The centre-right coalition government looks to be as committed to a broad EMU if it pulls off an unexpected victory. Philippe Seguin, tipped as the next prime minister if the centre-right win, called on Thursday for EMU to include Italy, Spain and Portugal from the start.
Economists polled by Reuters are expecting the franc to weaken no further than 3.40 per mark on a Socialist win, and to strengthen to no more than 3.3620 if the coalition retains power.
The German government's ability to resist pressure from a new French administration for a broad EMU has been reduced by the battle it is waging within its own borders.
The Bundesbank this week attacked Bonn's plans to revalue its assets, but Bonn said it would go ahead regardless.

"Germany can't fudge the criteria to such an extent that the Bundesbank is critical, but still expect to have the moral authority to keep other countries out," said Keith Edmonds at IBJ. "This will give the mark a softer bias."

That is not to say the mark will slump on its European crosses. For one thing, central banks are likely to be keen to prevent their currencies from strengthening too far away from their central parities against the mark in the European exchange rate mechanism.
Also, the prospect of a soft euro is more likely to spur traders to seek out markets which are completely insulated from EMU turbulence than to stock up on the peripheral currencies.

"You will either get a weak euro or else the whole thing will be delayed," said a trader at a Japanese bank in London. "It's unlikely that EMU will falter, so my bet would be to sell marks and buy Swiss francs."
He said the SNB would be powerless to deter such large flows into francs unless it resorted to slashing its discount rate, already the lowest in Europe at one percent.
